written: Written 28 Nov 2026. Figures in the tables update automatically; these summaries are refreshed separately.
themes: Shares bounce back after the sell-off

A week after US shares fell into a “correction”, they had their best week since April 2025. The S&P 500 rose about 5.6% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq about 6.7%, as AI and chip shares recovered. Gold and silver also rebounded. The calmer mood took some pressure off safe havens such as the yen.
Strong US data keeps a December Fed rise on track

US growth in July–September was revised up to 4.3% at an annual rate, and the Fed’s preferred core inflation measure (core PCE) rose to 3.3%, the highest in nearly three years. Jobless claims fell to 189,000. Futures put a quarter-point rise on 9 Dec at roughly 95%, and two rises are now fully priced by March 2027.
Most central banks still lean towards higher rates

Bank of England Governor Bailey told MPs further rises are more likely than not if energy prices stay high. ECB minutes showed many members see the case for another rise, and Bank of Japan board member Tamura called for faster rises. Markets put a Bank of Canada rise on 9 Dec at about 77%. Australia is the exception: despite inflation jumping to 4.9%, markets expect the RBA to hold.
The dollar stays near a 19-month high

The dollar index ended near 104, little changed on the week. The New Zealand dollar fell to about 54.4 US cents on 23 Nov, its lowest since 2009, and the euro dipped to about $1.088. The Canadian dollar recovered about 0.7% to around C$1.425 per US dollar. The dollar stayed just below ¥160, a level where Japan has stepped in before.
US bond yields steady; the gap between short and long yields narrows

The US 10-year yield ended the week near 4.94%, roughly unchanged. The 2-year yield, which tracks expected Fed moves, rose to about 4.72%, so the gap between the two shrank to its narrowest since February. After allowing for expected inflation, the 10-year “real” yield is still high, near 2.8%.
Oil steadies as attacks revive supply worries

Brent rose about 3% to $95.44, its first weekly gain in November, while WTI slipped about 1% to $83.08. A projectile hit a Saudi refinery at Jazan on 26 Nov and tankers near Hormuz were attacked. OPEC+ meets on 29 Nov and is expected to keep output targets for early 2027 unchanged.

USD.note: Held at 3.75–4.00% on 28 Oct; two members wanted a rise. Since then data has run hot (Q3 growth 4.3% annualised, core PCE inflation 3.3%), and futures put a quarter-point rise to 4.00–4.25% on 9 Dec at roughly 95%.

EUR.note: Held on 29 Oct (deposit rate 2.50%) after two rises this year. Minutes of that meeting, published 26 Nov, showed many members felt the data backed further tightening, and a rise to 2.75% on 17 Dec is widely expected.

GBP.note: Raised to 4.00% on 5 Nov, its first rise since 2023 (Catherine Mann wanted 4.25%). On 25 Nov Governor Bailey told MPs it is “more likely than not” rates must rise further if energy prices do not come down, and Mann said the best response is to raise “more and sooner”; markets put a rise on 17 Dec at about 80%.

JPY.note: Held at 1.25% on 30 Oct in an 8–1 vote (one member wanted a rise). Board member Tamura said on 26 Nov the bank must keep raising, possibly faster, as rates are still well below “neutral”; swaps put a rise to 1.50% on 18 Dec at about 80%.

CAD.note: Raised to 2.50% on 28 Oct, its first rise since July 2023, as oil pushed inflation up. On 24 Nov Governor Macklem said firms plan to pass more costs on to shoppers and that the bank would raise rates if inflation looks set to stay too high for too long; markets put a rise on 9 Dec at about 77%.

AUD.note: Raised to 4.85% on 3 Nov in a 6–3 vote (three wanted to hold), its fifth rise this year. October inflation then jumped to 4.9%, but with unemployment at 4.9%, markets still put a hold on 8 Dec at about 97%; some economists see a risk of a rise in February.

NZD.note: Surprised markets by holding at 2.75% on 28 Oct in a 4–3 vote (three wanted a rise). Governor Breman has warned fuel costs may be spreading into other prices, and markets expect a quarter-point rise on 9 Dec.

CHF.note: Held at 0% on 24 Sep and stands ready to sell francs if needed. Chairman Schlegel has said the bank “won’t hesitate” to act if inflation (1.5% in October) threatens price stability, but sees no broad spread of price pressure; the next decision is 10 Dec.

CNY.note: Lending rates unchanged again on 20 Nov (1-year 3.00%, 5-year 3.50%), the 18th month in a row; growth support comes mostly from the government. The central bank set its daily yuan rate at 6.7111 per dollar on 25 Nov, the strongest since April 2022.

stories.USD: The US economy is running hot. Growth in July–September was revised up to 4.3% at an annual rate, from 3.4%. Core PCE inflation, the Fed’s preferred measure (without food and energy), rose to 3.3% in October from 3.1%, the highest in nearly three years. Jobless claims fell to 189,000, well below the 201,000 expected, and new home sales jumped 14.2%. This all supports a Fed rise in December, which futures price at roughly 95%. Shares had their best week since April 2025, and the 10-year yield held near 4.94%. Next: ISM factory survey and job openings 1 Dec (UK 15:00), ISM services 3 Dec, November jobs report 4 Dec (UK 13:30), Fed decision 9 Dec, November inflation 10 Dec.
stories.EUR: Inflation is high at 4.0% (October), mainly because of energy; core inflation (without food and energy) was 2.6%. Business surveys held steady in November: the overall PMI stayed at 51.7 (above 50 means growth). Germany grew at its fastest pace in over four and a half years, while France largely stalled. Services were a little weaker than expected (51.2). Minutes of the ECB’s October meeting showed many members felt the data backed more tightening, and a rise on 17 Dec is widely expected. The euro dipped to about $1.088 on 23 Nov, its weakest since April 2025. Spain holds a general election on 29 Nov. Next: German inflation 30 Nov, euro-area inflation 1 Dec (UK 10:00), Lagarde speaks 2 Dec, unemployment 2 Dec, retail sales 4 Dec, ECB decision 17 Dec.
stories.GBP: UK inflation is 3.6% (October), pushed up by petrol, and the Bank of England is leaning towards another rise. On 25 Nov Governor Bailey told MPs a further rise is more likely than not if energy prices stay high, and called the economy “more resilient than we expected”. Deputy Governor Lombardelli and Catherine Mann also sounded worried about inflation. Markets put a 17 Dec rise at about 80%. Business surveys showed slightly slower growth in November (services 52.0, below the 53.0 expected). The Bank’s Financial Stability Report (26 Nov) warned that AI firms’ borrowing is “complex, circular and opaque”, and said about 6.5 million households face higher mortgage payments over three years. Next: Bank officials before Parliament 3 Dec (UK 14:15), rate decision 17 Dec.
stories.JPY: Prices in Tokyo, an early guide for the whole country, rose faster in November. Core inflation (without fresh food) climbed to 2.9% from 2.6%, the highest since July 2025, though a little below the 3.0% expected. Electricity and gas bills drove much of the rise. National core inflation was 2.2% in October. The economy stalled in Q3 (output flat), but the Bank of Japan sounds ready to raise rates: board member Tamura said on 26 Nov it should keep raising, possibly faster. Swaps put a rise to 1.50% on 18 Dec at about 80%. The dollar stayed just under ¥160, near ¥159, a level where Japan has stepped in to buy yen before. Next: retail sales 29 Nov (UK 23:50), Ueda speaks 30 Nov (UK 01:05), unemployment 30 Nov, BoJ decision 18 Dec.
stories.CAD: Inflation is 3.1% (October), driven by petrol, while prices without food and energy rose only 1.8%. On 24 Nov Governor Macklem warned that firms expect to pass more of their higher costs on to shoppers, and said the bank would raise rates if inflation looks set to stay too high for too long. Markets now put a rise on 9 Dec at about 77%, and most big Canadian banks expect one. The economy is slowing: economists expect Q3 growth of about 1.3–1.5% at an annual rate, down from 3.3%, and unemployment is 6.7%. The Canadian dollar hit about C$1.438 per US dollar on 23 Nov, its weakest in 19 months, then recovered to around C$1.425. Next: Q3 GDP 30 Nov (UK 13:30), November jobs 4 Dec, rate decision 9 Dec.
stories.AUD: Inflation jumped to 4.9% in October from 4.3%, the highest in three years and above forecasts. Electricity bills rose 25.2% on a year as government rebates ended, and fuel was up about 32%. The RBA’s preferred core measure (trimmed mean) rose to 3.8% from 3.6%. Even so, the jobs market is weak: unemployment is 4.9%, the highest since 2021, after two months of job losses. So markets still put a hold on 8 Dec at about 97%, though some economists now see a risk of a rise in February. Markets still see the next move as a cut, in 2027. The Australian dollar is near 66 US cents, close to its lowest this year. Next: household spending 30 Nov, Bullock speaks 1 Dec (UK 08:15), Q3 GDP 2 Dec (UK 00:30), RBA decision 8 Dec.
stories.NZD: Shoppers bounced back strongly: retail sales volumes rose 2.2% in the September quarter, more than four times the 0.5% expected and the strongest since 2021. Inflation is 3.7% (Q3), and markets expect the central bank to raise rates on 9 Dec. Unemployment is high at 5.7%, though. Final results of the 7 Nov election, released on 27 Nov, left Prime Minister Luxon’s three-party coalition with 65 seats, one short of a majority. The centrist Opportunity Party (7 seats) now holds the balance, so coalition talks may take time. The kiwi fell to about 54.4 US cents on 23 Nov, its lowest since 2009, as the US dollar rose. Next: ANZ business confidence 30 Nov (UK 00:00), RBNZ decision 9 Dec.
stories.CHF: Swiss inflation rose to 1.5% in October, the highest since late 2023, mostly because of fuel and heating oil; core inflation stayed low at 0.5%. An early estimate shows the economy grew 0.2% in Q3. The SNB keeps its rate at 0% and says it is ready to sell francs if the currency gets too strong, while Chairman Schlegel sees no broad spread of price pressure. Markets expect no change in December. The franc is a safe haven, so it can gain when global worries rise; it has weakened against the dollar this month as US rates look set to rise. Swiss voters go to the polls in referendums on 29 Nov. Next: full Q3 GDP and retail sales 30 Nov, November inflation 2 Dec (UK 07:30), SNB decision 10 Dec.
stories.CNY: China is shown because it drives AUD, NZD and commodity demand. Factory profits jumped 20.1% on a year in October, up from 14.4% in September, led by electronics makers riding the AI boom; profits are up 16% so far this year. But shoppers are cautious: October retail sales grew just 0.4% on a year, and property investment is down 21.6% so far this year. Consumer inflation is only 0.7%. Lending rates were left unchanged for an 18th month. The yuan is strong: the central bank’s daily rate hit 6.7111 per dollar on 25 Nov, the strongest since April 2022, helped by exporters swapping dollars for yuan before year-end. Next: official business surveys (PMIs) 30 Nov (UK 01:30).

oil.title: Oil (WTI and Brent)
oil.what: The price of crude oil. Brent is the global benchmark, WTI the US one.
oil.now: Brent ended the week at $95.44, up about 3% and its first weekly gain in November; WTI slipped about 1% to $83.08. Brent is about 8% below late May (about $104). Supply fears returned: a projectile hit Saudi Aramco’s Jazan refinery on 26 Nov, the Houthis claimed attacks on Ras Tanura, and tankers near Hormuz were attacked. There is still no US–Iran deal, and the US blockade of Iranian ports continues. On the other side, Gulf exports are recovering and the IEA expects supply to run ahead of demand. OPEC+ meets on 29 Nov and is expected to keep output targets for early 2027 unchanged.
oil.links: High oil helps oil exporters (CAD) and hurts importers (JPY, EUR). It feeds straight into inflation, which is why central banks have turned to raising rates.

gold.title: Gold
gold.what: Gold priced in US dollars. It pays no interest, so it competes with what investors can earn elsewhere.
gold.now: Around $3,650, up about 3.3% this week after its worst week since March, as shares recovered and bargain hunters bought. That is still about 19% lower than in late May (about $4,500) and roughly 35% below January’s record near $5,595. The headwind has not gone: a December Fed rise looks almost certain, the 10-year real yield is near 2.8% and the dollar is near a 19-month high. Central banks are still buying: they added a net 321 tonnes in Q3, according to the World Gold Council.
gold.links: Gold tends to rise when real yields fall, the dollar weakens or fear spikes. It often moves with CHF and JPY as a safe haven, and with AUD, since Australia is a big producer.

silver.title: Silver
silver.what: Half precious metal, half industrial metal (solar panels, electronics), so it swings more than gold.
silver.now: Around $43.70, up about 6% this week after hitting its lowest in over a year. It is still roughly 43% lower than in late May (about $76) and around 64% below January’s peak near $120. It faces the same rate headwind as gold; this week it was helped by the rebound in tech and AI shares, which eased worries about factory demand.
silver.links: Follows gold in direction but with bigger swings; weaker Chinese industry weighs on it.
